newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West threatens action over Bosnia refugee expulsion.
newsitem.headline: West threatens action over Bosnia refugee expulsion.

text.p: The West strongly condemned Bosnian Croat police and hardliners in the central Bosnian town of Jajce on Monday for the expulsion of hundreds of Moslem refugees who had recently returned to their pre-war homes.

At a news conference in Sarajevo representatives of several international organisations pledged to investigate who was responsible for orchestrating demonstrations which led to mobs of angry, drunken Croats driving Moslems from their homes by intimidation.
They also insisted any police or politicians found to be involved would be punished and removed from office.

"Without the return of minorities to their homes...the whole peace process could collapse. There can be no lasting peace and no stability in this country unless minorities are allowed to return to their homes," said Kris Janowski, spokesman for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

"It is quite appalling that these people were recleansed from their homes one year and nine months after Dayton, having been able to gather enough courage to go back there to their partially destroyed homes last week," he said..
Under the Dayton agreement which ended the Bosnian war in 1995 all refugees in the former Yugoslavia have the right to return to their pre-war homes.
"I can now add a new term, ethnic recleansing, to the lexicon of horror in Bosnia-Hercegovina," said David Foley of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe.

Late on Sunday the last 85 Moslems of hundreds who had returned to the Jajce area, about 100 km (60 miles) northwest of Sarajevo, left their village after a weekend of threats and intimidation from local Bosnian Croats.
They were escorted away from the village of Kruscica, 10 km (six miles) east of Jajce, by NATO-led peace troops.

One man was found dead in a burned-out house in Kruscica, Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the United Nations International Police Task Force (IPTF), told reporters. He said altogether around 500 Moslems had left the Jajce area over the weekend.

The Moslems intend to make another attempt on Tuesday to return to the villages where they lived before the 43-month Bosnian war. Janowski said the UNHCR would pressure local authorities to allow them to return.
"I simply don't know whether they can go back and how safe they are going to be. Considering what happened at the weekend they are not going to be very safe," he said.
Ivanko said the United Nations police force had begun an investigation into the role of local police in the events.

"On the basis of these investigations we are insisting that the perpetrators should be punished and those who are found to be politically responsible should be removed from office," said Simon Hazelock, spokesman for the international community's High Representative in Bosnia.
All conceded that local authorities and police were unwilling to accept the provisions of the Dayton accord.
"The tragedy of this country is that in many cases the local authorities...still pursue the same line that they pursued during the war," said Janowski.
"The problem is that belief in Dayton is a selective religion in some high places...(and) the commitment in Dayton to minority return is treated as a phoney commitment.
"If this philosophy prevails the whole peace agreement and by implication possibly even peace will be threatened."
The population of Jajce is around 98 percent Bosnian Croat, and the town is run by Croat authorities.
The NATO-led peace force in Bosnia insists local authorities are ultimately responsible for the safety of all people, including returnees.
Moslems and Bosnian Croats allied with each other in 1994 under a U.S.-brokered deal and are now joined in a Moslem-Croat Federation which makes up half of post-war Bosnia.
But the federation remains divided into largely Moslem and Croat-dominated enclaves with little cooperation between them.
